content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Previous works have tackled representation learning in multi-label and multi-modal setting, but have neglected to consider the common requirement of generalization to novel, and unknown, tasks at test-time. Authors propose an integrated multi-modal multi-label framework for Deep Metric Learning (DML), which we term 3ML–DML. The framework extends existing proxy learning losses from DML to the multi-label domain, and provides a novel method for enforcement of label correlations via these proxies. Authors also further introduce a multi-modal component which builds a standard fusion model but draws from DML literature in order to incorporate auxiliary, high-dimensional embeddings and feature spaces from each mode of data as context to match with and refine the output of the fusion model for further improvements in generalization performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The authors' reference lists are highly relevant and recent high-quality papers.
- The definition of the problem is clear, readers can easily understand authors how to solve the problem.
- The derivation of the formula is detailed, and the idea of the model is clear.
- Content of the manuscript is relevant to readers, since it discusses deep metric learning.
- The manuscript is technically sound as it shows and explains the evidence behind the authors' conclusion.
- The setup of the experiment is reasonable.

Weakness:
- Due to the short length of the article, the structure of the introductory section is not obvious. I suggest authors to divide the introduction into several parts such as motivation, limitation of prior works, challenges, our approach and contribution.
- Authors offer a shallow discussion of their results. It is not enough to just summarize the values. The author are advised to explore deeper reasons behind the values.
- From my point of view, I always divide train, val and test by 7:1:2 while authors seems to use 7:1.5:1.5 instead. Is there any special reason in data processing? Authors are suggested to explain this issue.
- In author's work, Pearson correlation coefficient in page 5 eq (3) is related to Euclidean distance. Can standardized Euclidean distance provide a better results?
- Texts in Figure1 such as multimodal and multilabel is strange, why the multi and modal or label is in different fonts? Please make a revise.
- Only one figure reveals the visualization of the 3ML-DML framework seems not enough, authors can consider add more figures for a more comprehensive demonstration.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes 3ML-DML, a deep metric learning (DML) framework for a multi-label, multi-modal setting. By extending a classical DML objective, namely ProxyNCA, to the multi-label setting, and adopting a well-established multi-modal fusion architecture, the proposed model can learn more informative representations. Additional losses such as regularizing with label correlation information, and auxiliary training objectives for multi-modal fusion are proposed. On two datasets, MIMIC-III and MM-IMDB, the proposed model is compared against baselines and ablations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper is well organized and mostly clearly written. The problem is clearly defined, and the proposed method is easy to follow. 
- The proposed approach, although not too novel, is formulated based on popular framework, and overall reasonable.

Weaknesses:
- The claimed contribution is not supported by the empirical results, only tenuoulsy at best. In Table 1, the performance gap between the proposed model and the baselines are either mostly negligible, or the proposed model shows worse performance than the baselines, especially when it comes to Recall@1, which is the indicator for the quality of the learned embeddings. It is even more concerning that this becomes worse when the models are evaluated on novel labels. In order to clearly demonstrate the merit of the proposed method, it would be necessary to performan a k-fold cross validation (as the entire dataset size is rather small), and perform a significance test between the proposed model and the baselines.
- Even the methodological contribution is very weak, given that the new components added in the paper makes little difference to the task performance. The ablation study in Table 2 shows that the modifications added to the previous works (ProxyNCA and Multimodal Bottleneck Transformer) do not have significant impact to the overall performance of the proposed model. This means that the essential working parts of the proposed model are ProxyNCA (with a straightforward extension for multi-label setting) and MBT, which indicates that the methodological contribution of this work is extremely weak, as opposed to how it is presented in Section 2 and 3.
- In contrast to the care and effort given to Section 2 and 3, the experiments and result discussion/analysis is extremely shallow and typo-ridden (e.g. "with the exception of COCO") . Several details are either missing, or brushed off to the appendix (but not actually there), and the only experiment results are quantitative performance comparison between different models. It would be more persuasive if the paper focused on only one dataset, and performed a more in-depth analysis of the learned embeddings of each modality, and each proxy, and how different methods affect the learned metric space, along with some visualization.
- Lack of experiment details. For example, the paper states that the Multimodal Bottleneck Transformer (MBT) was used, but fail to specify the size of the bottleneck, etc. The paper says the details are provided in the appendix, but they are nowhere to be found.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Up to Section 3, the organization is well structured and writing is clear.

Quality: The overall quality of the experiment section needs more improvment, given how well-written Section 1, 2, and 3 are. The paper has potential, but empirical execution leaves a lot to be desired.

Novelty: The paper addresses an interesting and important problem, but the empirical execution does not support its claim.

Reproducibility: All the details of the experimental setup and implementation are nowhere to be found, severely hurting reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper starts strong by addressing an interesting and important problem, and deriving a reasonable solution, but the experiment part leaves a lot to be desired, and cannot support the main claim of the paper.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

display_title: Official Review of Paper5902 by Reviewer Sgaq

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a Deep Metric Learning (DML) framework for multi-modal multi-label data. The framework draws upon an existing proxy learning loss function and extends it to the multi-label learning case by accounting for label correlations. In addition, the framework learns latent feature representations from multiple data modalities (or modes) and fuses them into a single joint representation; such that the representation of each mode is allowed to influence and thus refine the fused representation. When applied to two multi-modal multi-label applications coming from two different domains, the authors suggest that the proposed framework yields improvements (in terms of multi-modal multi-label performance as well as zero-shot generalization to new labels) over naive multi-label metric learning and supervised multi-label learning approaches.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

* The authors extend the ProxyNCA loss to the multi-label case by learning a proxy representation for each label and minimizing the distances between the samples’ embeddings and the representations of proxies corresponding to the samples’ associated positive labels, while repelling the remaining proxy representations.

* Although considerable research has been conducted on DML approaches to quantifying similarity in high-dimensional spaces, such approaches are primarily designed for single-label unimodal settings. This work appears to be the first to leverage a label correlation loss to enforce similarities among labels in multi-label data characterized by multiple modalities.

* As opposed to existing metric learning methods for multi-modal data that are typically limited to conventional metric learning for highly specific domains, the proposed framework aims to combine and jointly learn from multiple modes by (1) optimizing a separate multi-label MultiProxyNCA objective while capturing relations between different samples in each mode, and (2) performing a contrastive similarity-based self-distillation (S2SD) of mode-specific embeddings into a single fused embedding.

* The authors combine the above three points into a comprehensive objective function that (1) is aware of the multi-label setting by learning a proxy representation for each label, (2) captures and distills unimodal relations that may exist between samples into the multi-modal space, and (3) leverages correlations among different labels. In addition, the authors propose a unified method, referred to as multi-modal multi-label deep metric learning (3ML-DML), to optimize the aforementioned joint objective function.

* The proposed framework is applicable to tasks which require generalization to new and unobserved labels, a setting which is not addressed by current representation learning approaches for multi-label and multi-modal data. 

* The effectiveness of the proposed 3ML-DML method has been assessed on two real-world tasks involving multi-modal multi-label data: a clinical phenotype prediction task from the healthcare domain, and a movie genre prediction task.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Weaknesses:

* In the related work, the authors mention that “classic multi-label embedding methods are prohibitively slow (Liu & Tsang, 2015a; Bhatia et al., 2015), so recent works have induced sparsity in embeddings (Shen et al., 2018) or select features directly (Gonzalez-Lopez et al., 2019).” However, the authors fail to discuss or refer to any extreme multi-label (XML) approaches, which are specifically designed to address the efficiency of multi-label methods in general and their challenges of scalability to a large number of labels. Moreover, due to their relevance to multi-label tasks, XML methods could have been also considered among the baselines by simply applying them to each mode separately. I would encourage the authors to elaborate in their response on why such methods were not discussed and considered for comparison with the proposed framework.

* In the related work, the authors also discuss that the fusion operation can range from concatenation to more complex model-based or attention-based fusion. Nevertheless, apart from the comparison with concatenation-based fusion, the authors have neither compared their 3ML-DML method with multi-modal methods relying on other fusion operators nor have they assessed the impact of different fusion operators on 3ML-DML’s performance. I would suggest that the authors provide an explanation as to why additional fusion operators were excluded from the study.

* Although necessary for learning from multi-label data, the extension from Eq. (1) to Eq. (2) is rather natural and straightforward as it simply generalizes the concept of a proxy (from learning class-specific to label-specific proxy representations); thus I do not believe that such an extension (or generalization) can be considered a novel contribution to DML for multi-label data.

* The authors do not discuss any relations or differences of their work to multi-view learning and what limits the applicability of multi-view approaches to the considered multi-modal setting. I would like to ask the authors if they could include a brief note on this in their response.

* Is the trade-off weight $\gamma$ in Eq. (6) the same as the one in Eq. (7)? If that is the case, then the same weight is applied to the label correlation loss as well as the two distances between the batch-wise similarity matrices. However, the former loss and the latter distance losses are not comparable and thus I am not confident whether the same importance weight can be applied to both. I would recommend that the authors discuss the choice of the weight for the two types of losses or, in case different weights were applied, then the notation should be revised accordingly in Eq. (6) and Eq. (7).

* Among the evaluation metrics, the authors could have considered additional metrics that measure the overlap between the positive labels of a given sample and the top-k labels that were predicted/retrieved as positive. Such per-sample metrics include Precision@k or nDCG@k. For more details on these metrics, I refer the authors to:

  K. Bhatia, K. Dahiya, H. Jain, P. Kar, A. Mittal, Y. Prabhu, and M. Varma. 2016. The extreme classification repository: Multi-label datasets and code. http://manikvarma.org/downloads/XC/XMLRepository.html 

  Note that these metrics are not to be confused with Recall@k (measured in the experiments) which the authors defined as the highest overlap in the *proportion of labels between a data point and its k-nearest neighbors* (not the top-k labels retrieved as positive for that data point).

* In Section 4.5, the authors state that the metrics were averaged “over two randomly chosen sets of labels for train/test label split”. I find this rather confusing. Were the data randomly split two times into datasets for training and testing and the metrics obtained on the two random spits were then averaged? If this is the case, I am wondering why the authors did not consider more random splits, i.e. trials of the same experiment (e.g., 10) to obtain a more representative estimate of the models’ average performances?

* From Table 1, it seems that 3ML-DML obtains either comparable or even slightly lower performance than the baselines, in terms of mAP and Recall@1. Even the claimed superior AUROC performances on the two datasets merely hold since the AUROC values obtained by the variants of the proposed approach differ by 1% or less compared to those obtained by the second-best performing baseline. Perhaps the effectiveness of 3ML-DML needs to be further assessed by considering additional datasets.

* The conclusions drawn from the generalization to novel labels are discussed in Section 5.1 from the perspective of the percentage drops in performance upon generalizing to previously unobserved labels; however, the original AUROC, mAP and Recall@k values are included neither in the main paper nor in the supplementary material. Thus, I would suggest that the metric values obtained by each method are included, at least, as a part of the Supplementary material.

* The conducted ablation study suggests that performance improvements from both S2SD and $\mathcal{L}_{corr}$ are introduced only on MIMIC-III, which I believe is not sufficient. For instance, as the authors already pointed out in Section 5.2., S2SD marginally degrades the overall AUROC on the MMIMDB dataset compared to standard fusion and the proposed multi-label ProxyNCA alone. The authors propose remedying this challenge by further exploring different representation dimensions for each modality expert in the multi-modal S2SD, however, no such analysis is included in the paper. As mentioned earlier in this review, perhaps the authors should consider additional datasets to obtain a better understanding of how the different components of 3ML-DML affect its overall performance.

* In Appendix C.1, the authors have analyzed the impact of the label correlation loss weight $\gamma$ on the AUROC and mAP of 3ML-DML and MPNCA. However, in all other experiments, the authors discuss performance in terms of AUROC, mAP and Recall@1. Thus, in addition to the plots for AUROC and mAP, I would suggest that a plot for the impact of $\gamma$ on Recall@1 is also included in Appendix C.1 for completeness.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Minor weaknesses:
There are also certain grammatical and typographical errors and remarks that require attention. Some of them are summarized as follows:
- Page 2, second paragraph: “metric presentation space” should be replaced with “metric representation space”.
- Page 2, fourth paragraph: replace “the” with “that” in “we demonstrate the 3ML-DML succeeds”.
- Page 2, fifth paragraph: “research ares” should be corrected to “research areas”.
- Page 4, last paragraph: “observed on each batch” should probably be “observed in each batch”.
- In Eq. (3), $d^2$ should not be written as a superscript. Consider replacing it with $(1-d^2/2)$. The same should be corrected in the supplemental section B.2 as well as in Eq. (4).
- On page 5 right after Eq. (3), it seems that “associated with” should be replaced by “denoting” or “representing”.
- Page 5, third paragraph: “multi-label tensor $\mathbf{Y}$” should be corrected to “multi-label matrix $\mathbf{Y}$” since $\mathbf{Y} \in$ {0,1}$^{b \times c}$ is two-dimensional.
- Page 5: Right after Eq. (5), the authors should describe what $\gamma$ denotes.
- Page 5, Section 3.2: In the phrase “a joint multi-modal representation $\psi^m$”, I believe that $\psi^m$ should be replaced with $\omega^m$.
- In the last paragraph of Section 3.2 on page 5, “to merge representation” should be corrected to “to merge representations”.
- In the last sentence of the first paragraph in Section 3.2.1, replace “singly” with “single”. In the same sentence, a word seems to be missing between “optimized with its” and “on instantiation”.
- I believe that the notations used in equations (e.g. Eq. (6)) should be explained in the main paper right after their respective equations (in addition to explaining them in the supplemental material) as this makes the paper difficult-to-follow.
- Page 6, right after Eq. (7): in the phrase “with $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}$ a weighting term”, include “being” right before “a”.
- In the first paragraph of Section 4.3, a word seems to be missing right after “linear classification downstream”.
- In Section 4.4, include “from” between “a linear layer mapping” and “the embedding space”.
- Page 9, Section 5.2: There is a sentence starting with “Thus, we conclude in our primary application dataset, we observe that each component provides improvement in the standard and zero-shot generalization case.” This sentence is rather confusing. It seems that the phrase “we conclude” should be removed from the sentence. I would like to ask the authors to revise it accordingly.
- In the supplemental section B.2, in the expression for $r$, the covariance between the vectors (i.e. the first sum over $k$) should be divided by, not multiplied with the two square roots representing the standard deviations of the two vectors. Please correct this accordingly.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
The paper is decently written, but there is certainly room for improvement when writing is concerned. The paper is well organized though, and technically detailed to a satisfactory extent. Apart from a few missing notation explanations, the notation is clear and consistent throughout the paper.

Quality:
The design and justifications for the proposed DML framework for multi-modal multi-label data seem to be technically sound. While most of the observations made regarding the performance of the 3ML-DML method seem to hold on the considered datasets, certain observations regarding 3ML-DML’s performance improvements need to be further supported by considering additional datasets (mentioned in the “Weaknesses” part of this review). Overall, the paper has merit but needs more work as it does not appear to be fully developed in terms of experimental evaluation.

Novelty:
From a methodological perspective, the contribution of this work can be considered rather incremental. In essence, the authors leveraged existing concepts from deep metric learning (proxy neighborhood component analysis and contrastive similarity-based self-distillation) and simply generalized them to multi-modal representation learning. The only contribution that can be considered novel in a certain sense would be the label correlation loss that, to the best of my knowledge, has not been leveraged in a multi-label multi-modal setting, although research on modeling label corrections has been done in the realm of extreme multi-label classification.

Reproducibility:
The experiments were conducted on two widely-used datasets which are publicly available. The code for the proposed 3ML-DML method is made available by the authors as a part of the supplementary files submitted along with the paper. That being said, reproducing the results of this work should be attainable.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work has merit but does not appear to be well supported experimentally. While this appears to be the first work to study an integrated multi-modal and multi-label setting for deep metric learning, the proposed method exhibits either comparable or, in some cases, slightly lower performance compared to the considered baselines. Also, this work is in need of a more extensive experimental evaluation that encompasses a broader range of baselines and additional datasets (among other weak points outlined in the “Weaknesses” part of this review). Overall, these weak points of the paper seem to outweigh its strengths. Therefore, I am not convinced that this work is a good fit for ICLR. Nevertheless, I am looking forward to the authors’ response and I would be willing to adjust my score in case I have misunderstood or misinterpreted certain aspects of the work.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
